t.tsugeer els@50.1,95.3:
In the far south of Tuva, a Russian republic on the border with Mongolia, sand dunes appear among the steppe and the mountains as if they had wandered north out of the Gobi. Tsugeer Els is one of these dune fields, near the village of Erzin, and it belongs to the Uvs Nuur Basin, a UNESCO site shared by Russia and Mongolia since 2003. The basin is a closed depression around the salt lake of Uvs Nuur, and within it you can find almost every landscape of Central Asia: glaciers, alpine meadows, taiga, steppe, semi-desert and sand dunes, all in a relatively small area.

The dunes here are a strange and beautiful sight, with pines and scrub growing on and around them, and the mountains of the Tannu-Ola range and the Mongolian highlands on the horizon. The wildlife includes argali sheep, snow leopards in the mountains, wolves, foxes and many birds of prey. Tuvans are a Turkic people with a strong tradition of herding, shamanism and Buddhism, and they are famous for throat singing, an extraordinary technique of producing several notes at once.

Riding here is a serious undertaking. Erzin is reached by a long road from Kyzyl, the capital of Tuva, which is itself a long way from anywhere; the main road is paved but often in poor condition, and beyond Erzin, tracks across the steppe and through the sand require off-road skills, good navigation and a capable bike. Sand riding is tiring and technical, and help is far away. Summers are short and can be hot, with sudden storms; winters are extremely cold.

At present, travel to Russia is restricted for many nationalities, and anyone considering a trip should check current official advice. The border with Mongolia nearby is open only at specific crossing points, and the area may require permits.

Erzin, around twenty kilometres away, has basic shops and fuel, but supplies can be unreliable; carry extra fuel, water and food. Kyzyl, home of the monument marking the supposed centre of Asia, is the main centre for services. In the villages, you may be offered salted milk tea and dairy products, and the hospitality of herders is generous. A night camping by the dunes, with a sky full of stars and the silence of the steppe, is an experience few travellers ever have.
t.poker creek@64.1,-141.0:
Poker Creek is as far north as most riders will ever cross an international border by road, and it has the feel of a place at the end of the world. The tiny US customs post sits on a bare ridge on the Top of the World Highway, a road that follows the crest of the hills between Dawson City in the Yukon and Chicken in Alaska, with views that stretch for a hundred kilometres across a sea of rolling, treeless mountains. Here the boreal forest thins out into tundra, and the light in summer is long and golden.

The border is open only in summer, usually from mid-May until mid-September, and hours are limited, so check before you go. Alaska time is an hour behind Yukon time, so you gain an hour as you cross. Carry your passport and make sure your documents are in order, because the officers are friendly but thorough. On the Canadian side the road is mostly sealed, and on the Alaskan side it turns to gravel for much of the way to Chicken, which has fuel and a famous cafe in the summer.

The village of Chicken got its name, according to the story, because the miners who settled it could not agree on the spelling of ptarmigan, so they picked something they could spell. Dawson City, on the Yukon side, is a Klondike gold rush town of wooden boardwalks and false-fronted buildings, and a free ferry takes vehicles across the Yukon River to the start of the highway.

Riding conditions are rugged. Expect gravel, loose stones and sudden weather changes, and be prepared for wind, cold and the possibility of snow even in summer. Fuel is scarce, so fill up in Dawson City and again at Chicken, and carry spare if your range is short. Distances are long and mobile coverage is poor. In return you get solitude, vast views and the sense of having ridden along the roof of the continent.
t.tok alaska@63.3,-143.0:
Tok is the first real town you meet in Alaska after crossing the border at Beaver Creek, and for riders who have spent a long day on the Alaska Highway it is a small and welcome sight. About twelve hundred people live here, spread along the highway at the junction of the Alaska Highway and the Tok Cutoff, which leads south towards Glennallen and Anchorage. The place calls itself the sled dog capital of Alaska, and the dogs, kennels and mushing history are genuinely part of local life.

The Alaska Highway was pushed through in 1942 as a military road, built by US Army engineers, including several segregated regiments of Black soldiers who did much of the hardest work, and a good share of civilian contractors. It links Dawson Creek in British Columbia with Delta Junction in Alaska. Tok sits near the end of it, and the highway here is paved, narrow and prone to frost heaves, those rolling buckles in the asphalt caused by the permafrost beneath. They are worth respecting, and hit at speed they can bite hard. Spruce forest closes in on both sides, and the mountains of the Alaska Range stand out far to the west on clear days.

From Tok, the Taylor Highway and the Top of the World Highway head north-east into Yukon Territory. The route climbs above the tree line, following ridges with long views over rolling tundra, and passes through the old gold-rush settlement of Chicken, which supposedly took its name when the miners could not agree on how to spell ptarmigan. The road is paved in parts and gravel in others, and the border crossing at the top is open only in summer, so check dates before you commit. Beyond it, a free ferry crosses the Yukon River to Dawson City.

Tok has gas stations, a few restaurants and a visitor centre, and everyone in town knows the next fuel is far away. Mosquitoes are fierce in summer, wildfire smoke can close roads, and the long summer light lets you ride well into the evening. Carry spare water, warm layers even in July, and a good tyre repair kit.
t.holmavik@65.7,-21.7:
Hólmavík is a small fishing village on the eastern shore of the Westfjords, and for many riders it is the gateway to the wildest part of Iceland. It sits on a little peninsula in Steingrímsfjörður, with a harbour full of boats, a church and a handful of colourful houses, and it has barely three hundred and fifty people. The landscape around it is stark and beautiful: low, rounded hills, deep fjords and bare, dark mountains beyond. In summer the light barely fades, and at midnight the sky glows orange over the water.

The ride here is a long one, since Hólmavík lies off the Ring Road, and to reach it you take Route 61 or Route 68 across a high moorland of lakes, lava and grass. The road is paved, but narrow and with few barriers, and the weather can turn quickly. In the Westfjords the tarmac gives way to gravel quite often, so check the road conditions and be prepared to slow down. The wind is a constant companion, and can be fierce on the exposed stretches.

The town has an unexpected claim to fame: a museum of sorcery and witchcraft, which tells the story of the witch hunts of the seventeenth century in the Westfjords. Almost all of those accused in Iceland were men, which is unusual in Europe, and the exhibits explain the local magic, including the grisly necropants, a pair of trousers made from the skin of a dead man that were supposed to bring wealth. It is a fascinating and slightly eerie place and a good way to spend a wet hour.

Fuel and food are available in the village, so it is a good place to fill up before heading north on Route 643 along the Strandir coast, where the road becomes gravel and the villages are few. Drangsnes, a short distance away across the fjord, has hot tubs on the shore where you can soak with a view of the island of Grímsey. The best time to ride here is June to August, when the roads are clear and the days are long, and the quiet and emptiness of the fjords are a reward in themselves.
t.blonduos@65.7,-20.3:
Blonduos is a small town of about a thousand people on the north coast of Iceland, where the glacial river Blanda runs into Hunafloi Bay. It sits right on the Ring Road, Route 1, and is one of the few places of any size in the long, empty stretch between Borgarnes and Akureyri. The river is milky grey-green with silt from the Highlands, and it divides the town into an old and a new part.

The church stands out first, a modern concrete building completed in the early 1990s that is shaped like a volcanic crater, with a design that is quite unlike the usual white wooden Icelandic church. The textile museum, which tells the story of Icelandic wool and home crafts, is worth a visit if the weather turns bad. In the old quarter near the river there are a few wooden houses and a small harbour, and out in the bay seals sometimes bask on the rocks.

Fuel is available here, which counts for a lot. Between the towns in the north, stations are widely spaced, so fill up whenever you pass one. The town also has a swimming pool with hot tubs, a supermarket and a few cafes, so it makes a natural stop at the end of the day. After a long ride, an hour in the hot pot is as good as it gets.

On the road from Myvatn, you cross the high, open country of the north, with wide moorland, the occasional farm and views toward the sea. The surface is good, with long straights and gentle bends, but wind is the real danger, as gusts can hit a motorcycle with surprising force, particularly on exposed stretches and crossing bridges. Weather changes quickly, so carry warm, waterproof gear even in summer.

In summer, the light never really fades, and you can ride until late in the evening. Horses graze in the fields beside the road, and the local lamb and fish are worth trying. Take your time and enjoy the quiet.
t.stykkisholmur@65.1,-22.7:
Stykkisholmur is the main town of the northern Snaefellsnes peninsula, home to about eleven hundred people and perched on a rocky headland that shelters a snug little harbour. It looks out on Breidafjordur, a broad bay scattered with hundreds of small islands, and the view over the water is its great asset. The town has a pleasing mixture of old wooden houses, painted in bright colours, and a modern church whose white concrete shape rises above the harbour like a great seashell.

One of the oldest buildings is the Norwegian House, built in the nineteenth century from timber imported from Norway, which now holds a museum of local history. The Library of Water, a quiet art installation filled with columns of glacier water, sits in a former library on the hill. A short walk from the harbour takes you up Sugandisey, a little basalt island joined to the town by a causeway, with a lighthouse and a view over the bay. Scallops are fished here, and you can often eat them at a local restaurant.

The ferry Baldur sails from the harbour across Breidafjordur to the Westfjords, calling at the island of Flatey on the way, and offers a useful shortcut if you are heading to that part of the country. Check the timetable in advance, and book a space for the motorcycle in summer.

Fuel is available in town, together with a supermarket, a swimming pool and a handful of cafes and restaurants, so this is the natural place to refuel before or after the peninsula loop. The roads into town, Routes 54 and 58, are good tarmac with some sweeping bends, long climbs and descents and wide views over the water. Look out for sheep, and take care in crosswinds, particularly along the coast.

If the weather is fine, spend an hour at the harbour or climb the little island for the view. Seabirds and seals are common, and the evening light on the bay is something you will remember for a long time.
t.budardalur@65.1,-21.8:
Budardalur is a very small settlement at the head of Hvammsfjordur in western Iceland, and it serves as the centre of the Dalir district, whose name simply means the Valleys. Only a couple of hundred people live here, but it is an important stop on the road, because the nearest fuel for a long distance is found here, along with a shop, a cafe and a few services. A small dairy is based in the town, and local cheese and skyr are a good thing to try.

The area has real historical weight. The sagas of the Icelanders are rooted here, and the Laxdaela saga, one of the greatest, is set in the surrounding valleys, with its story of Gudrun Osvifsdottir and her tangled loves. Further inland, at Eiriksstadir, stands a reconstruction of the farm of Erik the Red, the Norse outlaw who founded the first settlement in Greenland, and where, according to tradition, his son Leif Eriksson was born. The turf-roofed hall gives an idea of what a Viking-age longhouse looked like.

The riding in this part of Iceland is open and relaxed. Route 60 runs through broad valleys and over low passes, with a good surface, moderate traffic and a mixture of long straights and gentle bends. Beyond town, the road toward the Westfjords climbs over the pass of Brattabrekka, where the views over the valleys are wide and the weather can change very quickly. The gravel sections that appear on some parts of the route need extra care, particularly on a heavy bike.

The fjord is shallow and edged with mudflats, which attract plenty of birds, and in summer the green meadows are speckled with sheep and horses. The air smells of grass and salt, and the light across the water is soft and wide.

Fill the tank here before heading into the Westfjords, where fuel stations are much more widely spaced. Take a break, stretch and enjoy the quiet.
t.isafjordur@66.1,-23.1:
Isafjordur is the largest town in the Westfjords, with about two and a half thousand inhabitants, and it sits on a narrow gravel spit that juts into the fjord Skutulsfjordur, with steep mountains rising almost vertically on three sides. It was settled early as a fishing and trading port, and it grew rich on cod. The oldest part of town has some of the finest surviving timber buildings in the country, some of which date from the eighteenth century, and the Westfjords Heritage Museum is housed in one of them, with exhibits on fishing, boats and daily life.

The ride here is a journey in itself. The roads of the Westfjords wind around deep fjords, over steep passes and along cliffs, and many sections are gravel. The tunnel into Isafjordur, which links three valleys in a Y-shape, has a one-lane section with passing bays, so be ready to pull over and give way to oncoming traffic. Plenty of stops are worth making, including the great waterfall Dynjandi, which falls in a series of cascades down a mountainside and is easily one of the most beautiful in Iceland.

Weather is a real factor. Fog, rain and strong wind are frequent, and in winter heavy snow often cuts off the passes. Summer is the best time to ride, when the days are long and the light lasts almost all night, but even in July the temperature can be cold, so carry warm clothes.

In town, you will find fuel, a supermarket, a swimming pool, restaurants and a bakery, all within a short distance of each other, which makes it a comfortable base. Fish is the thing to eat, and the catch of the day is usually excellent. Every year at Easter, the town hosts a rock festival with a defiantly local name, and the place fills up with musicians and visitors.

This is a fitting place to finish a ride through the Westfjords, a remote corner of Iceland that few people visit and nobody forgets.
t.beaver creek@62.4,-140.9:
Beaver Creek is the last Canadian settlement on the Alaska Highway, a few kilometres from the American border and the westernmost community in Canada. It is a small place of motels, a gas station and a customs post, set among spruce, willow and low hills at the northern edge of the Kluane region, in country where the winter lasts for half the year and the temperature can fall below minus forty.

The highway itself is the story. In 1942, after Japan attacked Pearl Harbor and invaded the Aleutian Islands, the United States Army built the road in about eight months, pushing a pioneer track through muskeg and permafrost from British Columbia to Alaska. Crews working from the north and south met at Soldier's Summit, near Kluane Lake, in November of that year. The road was rough and has been rebuilt many times, but it still follows much of that line, and the mileposts that count down the distance from Dawson Creek are a quiet monument to the effort.

The ride from Haines Junction to here runs along the foot of the Kluane ranges, past the great blue bowl of Kluane Lake and the mountain wall of Kluane National Park, which holds Mount Logan, the highest peak in Canada, and some of the largest non-polar icefields in the world. The road is mostly paved, but frost heaves and patched gravel are common, and warning flags mark the worst sections. Wind off the lake can be violent, and the weather can turn from sun to sleet in an hour even in summer. Look out for bears, which are common along the verge, and for Dall sheep on the slopes above the lake.

Services are sparse. Burwash Landing and Destruction Bay have fuel, and Beaver Creek has a couple of stations, but distances between them are long, so top up whenever you can and carry spare fuel if your range is small. The border crossing into Alaska is just ahead, and the hours and requirements should be checked before you travel, since you will need your documents in order.

If the light is right, the dark spruce, yellow aspen and white peaks make a late-September ride something quite special, but the nights are cold and frost is likely.
t.erzin@50.3,95.2:
Erzin sits in the far south of Tuva, a small town of around three thousand people in a basin that opens towards the Uvs Nuur, the great salt lake that straddles the Mongolian border. The Uvs Nuur basin is a protected area of international importance, a sweep of dry steppe, salt flats, sand dunes and mountain edges that shelters rare birds and animals. Erzin itself is a modest administrative town with a few shops and a handful of low buildings, but it is the gateway to some of the emptiest scenery in southern Siberia.

The road here is a long ride south from Kyzyl across country that gets drier and wider with each hour. The surface is variable, with good stretches of asphalt alternating with broken sections, and the bends are few. Distances are large and the wind can be fierce, especially in spring and autumn, when it blows across the open plain and tests your grip. Summer afternoons can hit the high thirties, and the heat shimmers off the steppe, so carry far more water than you think you need. Nights are cold even in July.

Fuel is available in Erzin, but do not assume the pump will always have supplies, and keep a margin for the way back. The shops stock basics, and there are a couple of places to eat where the menu is short and the portions generous: meat dumplings, soup, flat bread and strong tea. Beyond the town, the track into the steppe is a matter for experienced riders with a reliable bike, as services all but disappear and mobile signal comes and goes.

What makes the area special is the sense of space. Yurts dot the plain, herds of sheep, goats and horses move slowly across the grass, and in the evening the light turns gold and orange over the hills. The Tuvan herders who live here have kept many of their traditions, and they are generally friendly to visitors who behave respectfully and ask before taking photographs. If you are lucky you may see an eagle riding the thermals above the steppe, and at night the stars are overwhelming. Here the border is close, so keep your documents handy and avoid wandering off toward the frontier without checking local rules.
t.ular@50.5,95.6:
Tuva is one of those places that makes you check the map twice. It lies in the geographic centre of Asia, in southern Siberia, a republic of high steppe and dry mountain ranges, with the Yenisei starting its long run north from here. Ular and the neighbouring sites belong to the Uvs Nuur Basin, a protected area shared between Russia and Mongolia and inscribed by UNESCO in 2003 for its mix of desert, steppe, mountain and wetland, all within a few hours' travel.

Dunes and sandy patches appear nearby, and Tsugeer Els, the sand massif beside it on the ride, is a surprise, a miniature desert with small trees growing in it. In spring it can be green, in July hot and dusty, by October it is already cold.

People here are Tuvans, traditionally herders, and the culture is steppe culture: felt yurts in the pastures, sheep, horses and yaks, and the throat singing called khoomei, which sounds like two voices from one person. Buddhism and older shamanic practice sit side by side. You may be offered tea or fermented milk at a herder's tent, and refusing outright is not polite.

For the rider, this is gravel and dirt country, with tracks that split and rejoin and become soft after rain. A bike with decent clearance and a rider who can read sand are needed. Check border zone rules before going, since this area lies near the frontier and travel permissions matter. Go between June and early September, and carry more water than you think you need.
t.top of the world summit@64.1,-140.5:
Somewhere past the last bend, the trees just give up. The Top of the World Highway, on the Yukon side, climbs out of the Klondike valley and follows a bare ridgeline for miles, with the sky enormous and the hills rolling away in every direction in tundra shades of rust, gold and grey. The listed height here is around 1,376 metres, which is not Alpine, but at this latitude it is well above the tree line and feels like the roof of the continent.

The road itself is the main event. It is paved in places and rough chip-seal or gravel in others, with soft shoulders, frost heaves and few guard rails. The highway starts from the ferry at Dawson City, which crosses the Yukon river in summer, and heads west toward the Alaska border at Poker Creek. In good weather the ridgetop riding is among the most memorable in the north, since you look down on both sides and can see weather coming from far away. In bad weather, fog and wet gravel make it slow and serious.

It is a summer road. The highway is generally closed in winter, and the border crossing keeps limited seasonal hours, so check these before setting off, because turning back at the line is a very long day. The history is gold: this country was the backdrop to the Klondike rush of 1898, and the old miners' trails run across the same hills. You may spot caribou, ground squirrels, and in the berry season, bears feeding on the slopes.

There is nothing at the summit, no pump, no cafe, no shelter, and no town within easy reach. Fill the tank in Dawson City before you cross on the ferry, and carry water and some food. Chicken, on the Alaska side, has seasonal services, but do not assume anything is open. Dress for cold wind even on a warm afternoon, and bring a layer you can add when you stop to take pictures, because the wind up here does not care what the valley thermometer said.
t.chicken alaska@64.1,-141.9:
Chicken, Alaska, is spelled that way because the miners could not agree how to spell ptarmigan. The story goes that the early prospectors on Walker Fork wanted to name the settlement after the willow grouse that gathered there, gave up arguing over the spelling, and settled on something they could all manage. The village has kept its sense of humour ever since, with a gift shop, a cafe and a good deal of cheerful chicken-themed signage.

It is tiny, with a handful of residents in winter, and it lives on summer travellers and a little gold mining. The old dredge sits on the creek, a lumbering relic of the days when companies chewed up the gravel with machinery. You can still pan for gold here, and some people do, while others have a slice of pie and watch the road. Services are seasonal, so do not assume that anything is open outside the summer months, but there is usually fuel and a place to eat in the high season.

The road in from the east, the Top of the World Highway, crosses the border at Poker Creek, the northernmost land border crossing in the United States, which opens only in summer and closes for the season in September. Check the dates and hours before setting off, and carry your passport. The Alaska side of the highway is rougher than the Yukon side, with gravel stretches and frost heaves, and it winds down from the ridge into the valley of the Fortymile River through forest of spruce and birch.

From Chicken the Taylor Highway continues south to join the Alaska Highway at Tetlin Junction, with fuel and food at Tok. Make that a goal for the day, and bring water, a spare layer and insect repellent, since mosquitoes in the valley can be fierce. In summer the sun barely sets, and the evening light on the river is long and golden, which is the best time to ride this road.
t.batang@30.0,99.1:
Batang lies on the edge of the Tibetan plateau, on a broad highland plain at about 2,600 metres, near the Jinsha river, the upper Yangtze, which forms the border with the Tibet Autonomous Region. The town is Tibetan in culture, with a large monastery, prayer flags on every hill and a population of Tibetan herders and traders, and it has been a staging post on the route between Sichuan and Lhasa for centuries.

The ride from Kangding to Batang on the southern branch of the G318 is a serious piece of high-altitude touring. The road climbs over passes of more than 4,000 metres, crosses grasslands where yaks graze and prayer flags flutter on every ridge, and drops into deep river gorges. It passes Litang, one of the highest towns in the world at around 4,000 metres, famous for its horse festival in August, when riders in colourful costumes race across the grass. The surface is mostly paved, but there are sections of roadwork and landslides, and the weather can change from sun to snow within an hour.

Altitude is the main challenge here. Take things slowly, drink water, and be aware of the signs of altitude sickness. The wind on the high passes is bitterly cold, even in summer, so bring warm gloves and layers. The light on the high grasslands is brilliant, and the sky is a deep blue, with the clouds low and fast. Wildlife includes marmots, eagles, and the odd fox trotting across the grass.

There are no large nearby towns, and fuel is a practical concern. Fill up in Litang and Batang, and carry extra if you can. Travel rules for foreign riders in China, including permits and guides in some regions, are strict and change often, so check before you go. Spring and autumn offer the clearest views, and the winter is cold and icy. A bowl of noodles or a cup of butter tea in a roadside tent is the best way to warm up.
t.dynjandi@65.7,-23.2:
Dynjandi is a waterfall that spreads like a bridal veil down the side of a mountain in the Westfjords, one of the most remote and least visited parts of Iceland. The water falls about a hundred metres in a series of steps, narrowing at the top to about thirty metres and widening at the bottom to about sixty, so that the whole thing looks like a great white fan, and at the foot of the main fall there are half a dozen smaller cascades, each with its own name, that you can climb past on a short path.

The setting is as good as the waterfall. Dynjandi pours into the Arnarfjörður fjord, a broad, steep-sided inlet with a few farms and a long, narrow coast road, and the sea beyond is often a deep, dark blue. The campsite at the bottom is simple, with a toilet block and a flat grassy field, and on a clear evening, with the waterfall roaring and the light turning the mountains pink, it is a wonderful place to stay. Fulmars nest on the cliffs, and arctic terns dive along the shore.

The road to Dynjandi is the real adventure. Route 60 crosses the high Dynjandisheiði moor from the south, a long gravel climb with bleak views and a steep, winding descent toward the fjord, and the surface can be loose, rutted and slippery after rain. The Westfjords are remote, and the weather can be fierce, with fog, rain and strong winds, so take care on the gravel and the blind bends. Summer is the only comfortable season, since many of the roads are closed or difficult in winter.

Fuel is the main practical concern. There is no station at Dynjandi, and the nearest large town is Ísafjörður, about thirty-eight kilometres away as the crow flies but much further by road, with a population of about 2,600. Bíldudalur and Þingeyri are smaller, with limited services. Fill up before you leave any town and carry spare if you can, since the Westfjords have long gaps between pumps. Bring waterproofs and warm layers, even in July, and keep an eye on the gravel.
t.hvammstangi@65.4,-20.9:
Hvammstangi is a fishing village of a few hundred people on the east side of the Vatnsnes peninsula in north-west Iceland, where the bay of Miðfjörður opens into the great Húnaflói. It is small, tidy and unhurried, with brightly painted houses facing a harbour full of small boats, and it is known for shrimp, a trade that kept it going for years. The thing to do here is look at seals. The Icelandic Seal Centre in the village tells the story of the harbour and common seals that haul out on the beaches around the peninsula, and the shore at Vatnsnes is among the best places in the country to watch them at rest on the rocks.

Out on the peninsula, the road loops around a rough, windy coast, and at its western edge stands Hvítserkur, a basalt stack shaped like a drinking animal, with white streaks of bird droppings that gave it its name. The farms along the way have views across the bay to the Strandir mountains, and in summer the fields hold nesting waders such as golden plover, snipe and redshank, whose cries follow you as you ride. The ring road, Route 1, passes just to the south, bringing the faster traffic.

Riding the loop is a lesson in Icelandic roads. The ring road itself is smooth tarmac with long straight sections and exposed crosswinds, and Route 711 around Vatnsnes is mostly gravel, with loose stones, washboard and sheep that wander freely. It can be slow going. Weather moves quickly, and fog off the sea can drop visibility to nothing, so dress for rain, wind and cold even in July. In the long light of June and July the evenings are glorious, and you can ride at midnight with the sun low over the water.

Hvammstangi has a fuel station and a small shop, and a few places to eat, including a café by the harbour that serves fish soup. It is the start of the Arctic Coast Way, a long route around the north coast, so the facilities are used to travellers. Stock up on what you need, because the distances between settlements in the north are long, and the next big town, Blönduós, is some distance east. Check the forecast, carry a warm layer and keep your tank topped up.
t.arctic coast way point 1@65.4,-20.9:
Hvammstangi is the small town on the western shore of the Miðfjörður that Icelanders treat as the start of the Arctic Coast Way, a long coastal route along the north of the country. It has around six hundred people, a harbour with working fishing boats and a shrimp-processing history, and a calm, practical atmosphere that makes a good first stop for a ride that gets wilder as it goes. There is fuel in town and a supermarket, and it is wise to use both before you set out, since the north is sparse.

The landscape nearby is the Vatnsnes peninsula, a thumb of land sticking out into the Húnaflói bay, famous for its seal colonies and a dramatic sea stack called Hvítserkur, which looks like a rock dragon drinking from the sea. The road around the peninsula is a mix of tarmac and gravel, and it is a rewarding if slow ride. Seals haul out on the beaches in summer, and there are viewpoints from which you can watch them without disturbing them; they are shy, so keep your distance and keep your engine noise down.

Iceland's Ring Road, Route 1, passes nearby on the way to Akureyri and the north, and it is generally well surfaced and straightforward, though wind is the real hazard. Gusts here can be strong enough to move a bike sideways, and crosswinds on exposed straights should be respected. Weather turns quickly even in summer, and a warm layer and waterproofs are essential. Riders from the continent are often surprised by how bare the country is: few trees, wide valleys and a horizon that feels immense.

The area has a farming tradition, with sheep and horses on every slope, and the Icelandic horse is a local speciality; they are small, sturdy and curious, and will often come over to the fence to look at you. If you need a coffee or a warm meal, Hvammstangi has a few simple places, and the local seal centre is a good way to learn about the animals. The light in summer lingers until after midnight, and a ride along the coast in the small hours has a beautiful, dreamlike quality.
t.westfjords route 60 and 61 point 2@65.1,:
Búðardalur is a quiet little settlement at the head of the Hvammsfjörður, in the Dalir district, where the long, green valleys of western Iceland run down to a shallow bay. There is not much to the village itself, a cluster of houses, a small harbour and a few services, but the district behind it is one of the most storied in the country. This is saga country, the setting of Laxdæla saga, one of the great medieval tales of love, jealousy and revenge.

The ride here from the south crosses a mixture of moorland, farmland and small passes, with long, open bends and wide views. The road is reasonably good, and traffic is light. The wind can be strong, and the weather changeable, so it is worth allowing extra time. In the evening the light across the fjord is soft and golden, and the whole district has a feeling of calm.

A few kilometres away, a reconstruction of the farmstead of Erik the Red, the Norse explorer who founded the first settlement in Greenland, stands on the site where he is said to have lived. His son Leifur Eiríksson, who is credited with reaching North America around the year 1000, is thought to have been born in this district. A visit to the turf-roofed longhouse, gives a vivid picture of Viking life.

Nature in the district is gentle. The slopes are green with grass and birch scrub, and the shallow fjord is full of birds, including eiders and waders. Icelandic horses graze in the fields, and in summer the air smells of hay and wild thyme. The long valleys are a good place for walking and fishing.

Services in the village are limited but include a shop and a place to eat, and it makes a good stop for coffee on the long road north. The next big stretch is toward the Westfjords, so allow time and check the forecast.
t.westfjords route 60 and 61 point 3@65.7,:
Dynjandi is the waterfall that makes riders forget about the road. It pours down a wide, steep slope at the head of Arnarfjörður in a shape like a bridal veil, narrow at the top and fanning out to some sixty metres at the bottom, and below the main fall a staircase of smaller cascades tumbles on toward the shore. The whole thing is around a hundred metres high, and from the car park it is visible long before you reach it.

The ride in is part of the Westfjords' reputation. Route 60 winds around the fjords and over the mountain pass of Dynjandisheiði, with long, open bends, big drops and grand views, and sections that are paved alternate with gravel in places, so check the current condition of the road before you set out. Fog, rain and wind are all possible, and the road can be slippery. Traffic is thin, and you may ride for an hour without seeing another vehicle.

The Westfjords are the oldest part of Iceland geologically, about sixteen million years old, and the mountains here are flat-topped and cut by deep fjords, shaped by glaciers over millions of years. The landscape feels different from the south, emptier and more austere. Settlements are small, based on fishing, and many of the old farms have been abandoned as people moved to the towns.

A short path leads up beside the lower falls to the base of the main one, and the spray can drench you on a windy day. The smell of wet rock and moss is strong, and in summer the slopes around are green with grass and dotted with mountain flowers. Arctic terns nest nearby, and are fierce about it.

There is a small campsite and a simple cafe near the falls in summer, but little else, and Ísafjörður, about thirty-eight kilometres away, is the main town of the area. Take your time here, and have a good look at the falls from below as well as from the car park.
t.westfjords route 60 and 61 point 5@65.7,:
Hólmavík is the main village of the Strandir coast, a long, thinly populated stretch of the Westfjords facing north-east to the Arctic, and it feels like a place where the road has to try a bit harder. The population is a few hundred, and the settlement clusters around a small harbour on the Steingrímsfjörður, with the mountains behind and the open sea ahead. It is an unusual place for a museum, but it has a good one.

The Museum of Icelandic Sorcery and Witchcraft, in the village, tells the story of the witch hunts of the seventeenth century, when Iceland, unlike much of Europe, burned mainly men, most of them accused of using runic spells. The exhibition is eerie and surprisingly humorous, and includes a pair of trousers made from human skin, a legendary charm said to bring wealth. It is the kind of place that you might not choose to visit, but you will remember.

The ride here from the south follows the shore of Hrútafjörður and then the coast, with long, open bends and wide views, while the road west climbs over the high moor of Steingrímsfjarðarheiði. The surface is generally paved, but some side roads are gravel, and the weather can be wild, with fog and strong winds. Traffic is very light, and sheep are the main hazard. The northern sections of the Strandir coast are quieter still, reached by a long, slow road with few services.

Nature on this coast is wild and open. Seabirds nest on the cliffs, seals bask on the rocks, and Arctic foxes live in the hills. Driftwood from Siberia washes up on the shore, carried by currents across the Arctic Ocean, and it was long a valuable resource for the people of this treeless coast. The air smells of salt, seaweed and wood smoke.

The village has a shop, a cafe and a place to stay, so it is a sensible stop, though choices are limited. Ísafjörður lies farther along the route. Come when the light is soft, and allow time for the museum.
t.kjolur highland road point 3@65.7,-20.3:
Blönduós is the place where the Kjölur finally lets you go. After a hundred and fifty kilometres or more of gravel, glaciers and nothing, the road drops into the green valley of the Blanda river, and the first farms and the first tarmac feel like a small miracle. The town sits at the river mouth, on the north coast of the Húnaflói bay, with a population of under a thousand and a quiet, tidy air, and it is a good place to recover.

The ride into town is a gentle one, with long, easy bends along the river and the surface improving with every kilometre, until you meet the Ring Road. The river is glacier-fed and silvery grey, and the valley is full of sheep, horses and old farms. Be careful of livestock on the road, and look out for the single-lane bridges. The wind off the bay can be brisk, and in early summer the fog sometimes sits on the coast.

The river divides the town in two, and the buildings reflect different eras. On one side are the older wooden houses, some of them from the early twentieth century, and on the other the more modern district, with a distinctive church designed in the shape of a crystal or a rock formation, a bold concrete structure that looks like nothing else in the country. The town also has a textile museum, with an exhibition of Icelandic handicraft, and a heritage centre with the history of the district's people.

Nature is characteristic of the north. The river is a famous salmon river, and anglers come here in summer, and the coast is rich in seabirds. Seals bask on the skerries, and the air smells of salt and wet grass. The light in the evening, with the sun sinking behind the bay, is soft and gold.

Blönduós has the services you would expect of a small town, with a shop, a petrol station, cafes and places to stay. Sauðárkrókur, farther along the coast, is another town for supplies. After the Kjölur, a hot meal and a clean bed are treats.
t.isafjor ur@66.1,-23.1:
The approach to Ísafjörður tells you everything about the Westfjords. Come through the long tunnel from the west or along the fjords from the east and either way you arrive between mountains that rise almost vertically from the water, flat-topped, layered and striped with old snow, and the town lies on a curved spit of gravel in the middle of the Skutulsfjörður, as if it had been placed there by hand. It is the largest town in the region, with a few thousand people, a busy harbour and an airport where the landing between the mountains counts as one of the most dramatic in Europe.

The town has been a trading post since the sixteenth century, and the oldest part, Neðstikaupstaður, has a group of timber houses from the eighteenth century that were used by Danish merchants under the trade monopoly. One of them houses the Westfjords Heritage Museum, with exhibitions about fishing and life in the region. Ísafjörður grew prosperous in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries on fishing, especially for cod and shrimp, and the town still has a strong fishing and seafood culture, with excellent fish restaurants.

The town also has a lively cultural life for its size. Every Easter it hosts a music festival, Aldrei fór ég suður, which means I never went south, a wry nod to the young people who leave for Reykjavík. In winter the surrounding mountains are popular with skiers. The Westfjords have suffered from avalanches, and in the 1990s two villages nearby were struck by deadly avalanches, a tragedy that led to the building of large defensive barriers above the towns.

Riding in the Westfjords is an adventure. The roads follow the coast around long fjords, often on gravel, with short climbs over passes and many kilometres of shoreline. Route 61, around the Ísafjarðardjúp, is long and winding, with spectacular views and very little traffic. The weather can be harsh, with fog, rain and wind even in summer, and distances between services are long. The tunnels are a relief in bad weather.

Ísafjörður has fuel, supermarkets, cafes, restaurants and accommodation. It is the place to rest, eat and prepare for the next stage of the journey, because beyond it the villages are small and the services are few.
t.kanchanaburi@14.0,99.5:
Two rivers meet at Kanchanaburi. The Khwae Noi and the Khwae Yai join on the edge of town to form the Mae Klong, and almost everything that made this place famous, and infamous, happened along their banks. Most people know it from a film title, but the bridge over the Khwae Yai is only one short piece of the Thailand–Burma Railway that the Japanese army forced through the jungle in 1942 and 1943, using Allied prisoners of war and a far larger number of conscripted Asian labourers. Tens of thousands of them died, and the line earned its other name, the Death Railway.

It is worth giving the history an hour before you think about lunch. The Kanchanaburi War Cemetery sits right in town, immaculately kept, rows of low bronze plaques under rain trees, and the railway museum beside it explains the scale of the thing better than any bridge photo. Walking across the bridge itself is allowed, carefully, between the occasional tourist train. Early morning is the time: the light is soft, the vendors have not set up yet, and the river is still.

The ride out from Bangkok is not the attraction. Route 4 and then Route 323 run west through flat, hot country of sugar cane and roadside stalls, with trucks and a fair amount of traffic until Nakhon Pathom falls behind. Keep in mind that motorcycles are not allowed on Thailand's expressways and motorways, so the ordinary highways are your world. Once you are past Kanchanaburi, though, things improve. Route 323 follows the Khwae Noi valley north-west towards Sai Yok and Hellfire Pass, with limestone hills closing in and the traffic thinning, and the side road towards Erawan National Park and its terraced turquoise falls is a lovely detour of an hour or so.

For a food stop the town makes things easy. There are floating restaurants on rafts along the river, plenty of noodle shops on the main streets and a night market where you can eat for very little. Fuel is everywhere, from big branded stations to roadside pumps. Drink more water than you think you need: from March to May the heat in this valley is serious, and the best riding hours are the first three of the day and the last one before dark, when the hills turn blue and the river picks up the sunset.
t.phetchaburi@13.1,99.9:
Phetchaburi is one of Thailand's old royal cities, and its skyline is defined by a hill. Phra Nakhon Khiri, known locally as Khao Wang, rises just west of the town centre, its summit crowned by a nineteenth-century palace built for King Mongkut, Rama IV, a mix of Thai, Chinese and European styles, with white chedis and a small observatory where the king, a keen astronomer, studied the stars. A cable car runs up the hill, and the monkeys that live on its slopes are notorious for grabbing anything shiny or edible, so keep your belongings close.

The town itself is pleasantly unhurried, with old wooden shophouses, temples and a river running through the centre. Wat Mahathat Worawihan, with its five tall white prangs, stands out even in a province full of temples. A few kilometres north, the cave temple of Khao Luang is filled with Buddha images, and on sunny mornings shafts of light fall through openings in the roof, creating a magical atmosphere.

Phetchaburi is famous throughout Thailand for its desserts, many of them made with palm sugar from the sugar palms that grow in the surrounding fields. Khanom mo kaeng, a baked custard made with coconut milk, eggs and palm sugar, is the local speciality, and roadside stalls sell it everywhere. It is worth stopping to try.

As a fuel stop, Phetchaburi is ideal. The town has plenty of fuel stations along Phetkasem Road, Highway 4, the main route south from Bangkok towards Hua Hin and the peninsula, as well as restaurants and convenience stores. The highway is wide and fast, but it carries heavy traffic, including trucks and buses, and motorcycles are expected to keep left. Leave the highway for the smaller roads west of town, towards the forested hills of Kaeng Krachan, and the landscape becomes greener and more varied, with palm groves, rice paddies and limestone hills. The best time to ride is the cool season, from November to February.
t.kaeng krachan@12.9,99.6:
Kaeng Krachan is the largest national park in Thailand, a vast, rugged expanse of rainforest along the Tenasserim Hills on the border with Myanmar, and in 2021 the forest complex it belongs to was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site. It is home to elephants, leopards, gaurs, gibbons and hornbills, as well as an astonishing variety of butterflies, which gather in clouds on the damp sand along the streams. It is one of the wildest places in the country, and you can feel it as soon as you enter.

Your lunch stop is near the park headquarters and the great reservoir formed by the Kaeng Krachan Dam, whose blue waters, dotted with forested islands, stretch away into the hills. There are restaurants, resorts and homestays around the reservoir, catering to visitors to the park, and lunch there comes with fish from the lake and views of the mountains. Food and drink are simple but satisfying.

Inside the park, a road climbs deep into the forest to Phanoen Thung, a viewpoint famous for its sea of mist at dawn, when the valleys fill with cloud and the mountain peaks rise like islands. The road is narrow, steep and partly unpaved, and it is usually closed during the rainy season, roughly from August to October, when it becomes too muddy and dangerous. Even in the dry season, access may be controlled, with vehicles allowed up and down only at set times, so check with the park office before setting out.

The roads to Kaeng Krachan from the coast are pleasant, crossing farmland, orchards and pineapple fields before reaching the forested hills. They are generally quiet, with gentle curves and good surfaces. Fuel can be found in the villages near the reservoir, but there is nothing inside the park, so fill up beforehand; Tha Yang, about twenty-eight kilometres away, is the nearest larger town. The best time to visit is the cool season, from November to February, when the weather is dry and the mornings are fresh.
